framework: AP Research (AP Capstone) Course and Exam Description (effective fall 2024)
subject: Research (AP Capstone)

source.licence: © College Board; structure + our own wording only

outcomes.text: Place a problem or issue in context and identify its complexities
Others' perspectives prompt new questions; inquiry starts by narrowing interest, finding the problem and its origins, and situating it in a larger context
Ask questions and seek answers reflecting multiple, divergent or contradictory perspectives
Good research questions account for the complexity of the issue
Inquiry uses curiosity and imagination to explore approaches to complex issues
Identify a topic of inquiry
Topics come from personal interest, passion for a field, wanting to understand more, or addressing a real-world issue
Explore the knowledge base and perspectives, then adjust scope to the project's limits and resources
Inquiry reveals connections that raise curiosity and further questions
Explain the purpose and significance of scholarly inquiry
Scholars explore, explain and create
Inquiry addresses practical, theoretical, interpretive or aesthetic problems, or confirms, challenges or extends ideas
Situate inquiry within the scholarly community it matters to
Develop and revise a focused research question or project goal
The question or goal grows from the scholar's purpose
Questions usually need several revisions for scope and feasibility

topics.title: EU 1.2 Building on what is known

outcomes.text: Retrieve, question, organise and use prior knowledge about a topic
Understanding comes from experience, sources, culture and assumptions, not just collecting information
Brainstorming, concept maps, prewriting and drafting help organise and connect ideas
Inquiry confirms or challenges existing understanding and assumptions
Access and manage information with effective strategies
Information comes from secondary sources and from primary sources such as original works or collected data
Online databases and libraries hold secondary and some primary sources
Advanced search tools, Boolean logic and keywords refine searches
Source bibliographies can lead to more resources
Social media can be a source if its limitations are understood
Citation and reference software helps manage sources and bibliographies
Survey and statistics tools help collect and analyse large data sets

topics.title: EU 1.4 Relevance and credibility of sources

outcomes.text: Evaluate the relevance and credibility of sources and data for the inquiry
Research scope, purpose and source credibility affect the generalisability and reliability of conclusions
Credible evidence comes from relevant, reliable, current and authoritative sources
Judge credibility by the author's reputation, perspective and methods, and peer review
Survey data accuracy depends on respondent honesty and memory and on instrument design
Identify the information needed for the inquiry's context
How a problem is framed guides the information and methods needed
Design, plan and carry out a scholarly inquiry
Align methods of collection, analysis, innovation or interpretation with the question or goal
Methods may be qualitative, quantitative, mixed, or artistic processes
Adjust the course, tools and methods as scope and feasibility become clear
Artistic processes combine research methods with shaping media and form
Choose qualitative, quantitative or mixed data collection to fit the question
Analyse data in ways suited to the inquiry
Justify the sample chosen and know the limits of conclusions drawn from it
Use descriptive or inferential statistics to display and analyse data
Code and categorise data to find patterns or themes
Combine qualitative and quantitative data to triangulate trends and patterns
Show perseverance by setting goals, managing time and working independently
Plan methods and activities around deadlines, priorities, risks and others' availability
Expect setbacks, keep to essential goals and try alternatives
Seek expert guidance while staying self-sufficient
Use ethical research practices
Researchers have ethical and moral responsibilities
Laws and rules govern research on humans and animals, including institutional review board approval
Copyright and patent rules govern use of others' work and information
Use suitable reading strategies and read critically for a purpose
Read closely for main idea, tone, assumptions, context, perspective, reasoning and evidence
Preview and prioritise text by skimming, scanning, rereading and questioning
Make meaning by annotating, note-taking, highlighting and reading aloud
Perspectives are shared through written, spoken, visual or performance texts and include attitude or tone
Summarise and explain a text's main idea or aim without oversimplifying
The main idea sits in the thesis, claim or conclusion, or is implied
Artistic works convey a perspective; analyse context, subject, structure, style and aesthetic

topics.title: EU 2.2 Evidence and reasoning in arguments

outcomes.text: Explain and analyse the logic and line of reasoning of an argument
A line of reasoning is claims justified by evidence
Reasoning is organised by purpose, such as causality, definition or solution
Distinguish inductive reasoning from deductive reasoning
Missing the complexity of an argument leads to oversimplification
Strong arguments acknowledge and answer other arguments with concession, refutation or rebuttal
Evaluate the relevance and credibility of evidence in context
Context and situation relative to other arguments shape interpretation
Qualitative and quantitative evidence vary in validity
Authors choose evidence strategically
Writers may appeal to or manipulate readers through language, authority, qualifiers, fallacies and emphasis
Evidence can show comparative, causal or correlational relationships and trends
Credibility drops when authors ignore limitations, opposing views or their own biases
Evaluate the validity of an argument
An argument is valid when reasoning and conclusion align logically
Validity needs evidence aligned with conclusions and acknowledged limits
Conclusions are contextual and must be affirmed, qualified or refuted
Evaluate and critique others' inquiries, studies, works and perspectives
Judge studies on internal coherence and alignment of purpose, goals and methods
Connect an argument to broader issues through the implications of its claim
Arguments' consequences may be intended or unintended
Evaluate potential resolutions or solutions raised by an argument
Arguments can change behaviour and have real-world impact
Identify, compare and interpret multiple perspectives or arguments on an issue
Perspective is shaped by background, assumptions, worldview and outside sources
Perspectives may concur, complement or compete
Some perspectives are ambiguous, so interpretation may not give a definite answer

topics.title: EU 3.2 Not all arguments are equal

outcomes.text: Evaluate alternate, opposing or competing arguments by their implications and limitations
Arguments may appeal to emotion, values, bias, assumptions and logic
Consider how your own biases and assumptions influence judgment
Build a well-reasoned argument that accounts for the problem's complexity
Effective arguments use reason and evidence to convey a perspective stated in the thesis or conclusion
Carefully chosen, connected claims, reasons and evidence unify an argument
Qualifiers limit a claim and avoid overgeneralising
Answer other arguments with concession, refutation or rebuttal
A line of reasoning is a clear logical path to a conclusion
Reasoning can be deductive or inductive
Organise the line of reasoning by the argument's purpose
Arrange claims and evidence spatially, chronologically or by importance to show relationships
The same argument can be organised differently for different audiences
Choose a process aligned with the inquiry or project goal
Articulate your choices, even where they leave ambiguity
An aesthetic rationale is a reasoned argument for formal and stylistic choices in an artwork
Select and apply a disciplinary or interdisciplinary approach to a scholarly argument or aesthetic rationale
Each discipline has its own conventions for knowing, questioning and communicating
Use discipline-specific terminology in analysis
Foundational texts reveal a discipline's ways of knowing and valuing information
Disciplines can be broad, narrow, intersecting or combined
Interpret, use and synthesise qualitative and quantitative information from varied sources to support an argument
Evidence comes from print and nonprint sources, experts and field data
Compelling evidence is sufficient, accurate, relevant, current and credible
Choose evidence by context, purpose and audience
Selected and attributed evidence builds your argument's credibility
Write insightful commentary that links evidence with claims
Commentary connects evidence to the claim by interpretation or inference, patterns, trends and relationships
Attribute knowledge and ideas accurately and ethically with a citation style
Accurate attribution enhances credibility
Avoid plagiarism by acknowledging sources thoroughly
Introduce, integrate or embed source material in the argument
Cite quoted and paraphrased material following a style manual
Disciplines use specific style guides such as APA, MLA or Chicago
Appropriation in art has legal and ethical implications
Extend an idea, question, process or product to create new understanding
Innovative solutions challenge assumptions, imagine alternatives and use reflective skepticism

topics.title: EU 4.5 Consequences of arguments and choices

outcomes.text: Offer resolutions or solutions based on evidence, limitations and implications
Weigh advantages and disadvantages of options against the goal in context

units.title: Big Idea 5: Team, Transform, and Transmit

outcomes.text: Plan and produce a cohesive academic paper for an audience, context and purpose
Present conclusions with introduction and gap, method, results, discussion, conclusion and bibliography
Achieve coherence with logical flow and transitions
Follow conventions of grammar, usage, style and mechanics
Express tone through word choice, sentence structure and imagery
Vary sentences for emphasis with agreement, modifier placement and tense consistency
Precise word choice cuts confusion and wordiness
Spelling and grammar errors weaken credibility
Communicate through suitable media using effective design
Headings, layout, illustrations and captions aid engagement when used well
Present data graphically to aid understanding
Choose the medium by context, purpose and audience
Adapt an argument to context, purpose and audience
Adapt by selecting and emphasising information for audience, situation, medium and purpose
Explain choices in non-specialist language for outsiders
Engage an audience with effective delivery or performance
Vary volume, tempo, movement, eye contact and energy to emphasise and engage
Present work in discipline-specific or cross-disciplinary forms
Present after revision and rehearsal, using feedback and self-critique
Defend inquiry choices and the final product with clarity and conviction
Explain the rationale for choices in relation to the finished work
Respond thoughtfully to audience critiques and questions
Contribute individually to a collaborative effort
Sharing your strengths and challenges makes contributions more effective
Build a constructive team climate, resolve conflicts and include all members
Teams are built around tasks; low-risk teambuilding helps
Teams work best when they understand their diverse perspectives, talents and skills
Use interpersonal communication, consensus building, conflict resolution and negotiation
Consider online collaboration tools
Reflect on and revise your writing, thinking and creative processes
Reflection is ongoing and may use journals, self-questioning or drawing
Learning needs iterative rethinking, revising and rewriting
Stay mindful of the rationale behind chosen methods
Reflect on how inquiry deepened understanding and self-direction
Reflect on collaborative experiences
Note how actions and assumptions helped or hindered group and individual tasks
Reflect on the larger significance of the inquiry process and finished work
Explore future directions for inquiry and scholarship
Inquiry can transform understanding and one's identity as a scholar

topics.title: EU 5.4 Scholarly community and peer review

outcomes.text: Give constructive peer review suited to a project's stage
Peer review follows guidelines and criteria suited to the work
Receive and consider peer review of your work
Peer review sharpens your critical eye and your work
Scholarly communities do best when members seek and give feedback
